Hi Hannah,

Thanks for taking this on. Acme's security team is going through the SIG and we hit a few items that need additional clarity specific to Redwood's Dedicated GPU offering. The two main topics are: (1) tenant isolation on shared hardware (noisy neighbor risk, preemption, scheduler behavior) and (2) evidence that customer data/VMs/processes cannot access other tenants' model state or KV caches.

Our review would be satisfied with: an architecture sketch for Dedicated (GPU tenancy boundaries), a short test summary showing worst-case co-located workload impact, and any kernel/container-level config you enforce. We can accept redacted logs if there are hostnames or internal IPs.

Can you point me to an existing SIG spreadsheet answer (we already have the base SIG) and attach the architecture diagram and any test logs you can share? We have a compliance cutoff of 2026-04-09 for procurement.

Thanks,

Hi Alice —

Appreciate the clear ask. I'm attaching a short package that should address your review: redwood-dedicated-tenancy-architecture.pdf and isolation-test-summary.csv (both redacted). High-level answers below; I'll loop in Rohan for the deep technical bits and logs you requested.

- Tenancy model: Redwood Dedicated offers isolated allocation of GPU compute resources per customer. By default, a Dedicated capacity unit maps to a physical GPU assigned to that customer's inference worker processes (no co-located customer processes on the same GPU). For customers who explicitly request GPU multiplexing (to reduce cost), we support NVIDIA MIG partitions on A100-class hardware; that option is documented and requires explicit configuration in the order/contract.

- Noisy-neighbor / scheduler behavior: We schedule inference containers to avoid colocating separate tenants on the same GPU unless MIG has been elected. Preemption only occurs within the customer's own allocation (e.g., autoscale-managed worker replacement). We do not run multi-tenant model processes in the same container or user namespace.

- KV cache & model state: KV caches are held in process memory and ephemeral on the worker; they are never written to shared persistent volumes. We explicitly wipe cache memory on worker recycle. Model weights are mounted read-only from immutable artifacts; no writeable model areas are shared between tenants.

- Kernel/container controls: Standard runtime cgroups and namespaces are enforced; containers run in user namespaces where possible. Network segmentation is implemented at the VPC/subnet level so customer data paths are isolated. Encryption in transit (TLS 1.2+/mTLS for control-plane hooks) and at rest (customer data store) are in place. SOC 2 controls relevant to change management and access control apply to Dedicated.

Next steps: Rohan will provide a technical appendix with the specific kernel/cgroup settings and the raw test run logs (redacted as requested). If useful we can also schedule a 60-min deep dive with your infra team.

Regards,

Hannah — looping in technical detail and attaching the raw redacted logs: gpu-noisy-neighbor-run-20260329.log and kernel-cgroup-config.txt.

Quick summary of the key points for Alice's team: 
- MIG vs single-GPU: On A100 with MIG enabled, the GPU is partitioned into isolated instances with separate hardware contexts. Those partitions have their own compute and memory allocations; they still share the host PCIe fabric and NVLink topology, so extreme PCIe-saturating workloads can impact host-level throughput. We mitigate by not placing high-bandwidth batch jobs on hosts that host latency-sensitive tenants and by using placement policies that respect historical throughput.

- Host-level resources: We monitor host PCIe and host memory pressure and will prevent new placements if thresholds are crossed. In practice the majority of noisy-neighbor effects we've observed come from misconfigured batch workloads; Dedicated defaults are conservative.

- Benchmarks/logs: Attached log contains timestamped p50/p95 numbers from our synthetic noisy-worker experiments and a columned view of kernel cgroup settings used for the runs. We ran the isolation test with: 1) isolated worker (no other tenants), 2) MIG partitions (4-way on A100) with a noisy synthetic batch workload, and 3) single-GPU with co-located containerized workload.

- ECC/errors: ECC memory is a hardware-level feature; error correction is per-device. We surface device error counts and will evacuate capacity if persistent ECC events are detected. There is no mechanism for one tenant to inject ECC faults into another tenant beyond causing device-level stress that triggers hardware error counters.

Notes on redaction: logs are redacted to remove hostnames, internal IPs, and trace IDs. We can provide a side-channel verification (MD5 of raw log) if you require integrity proof.

If Alice's team wants more granularity we can run an additional tail-focused test during a reserved maintenance window.

- Rohan
